ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows an ideal operational amplifier circuit, with the non-inverting “+” input terminal grounded through resistor R; the inverting “-” input terminal receives input current Ix and is connected to the output terminal u0 through the upper feedback network. The feedback network contains R1 and R2, and the moving terminal of switch S is connected to the output terminal u0; when S is connected to terminal a, the output is fed back to the inverting terminal through R1; when S is connected to terminal b, the output is fed back to the inverting terminal through R2 and R1 in series. Reasoning: Under linear negative feedback, an ideal op-amp has a virtual short, and the “+” terminal is grounded, so the potential of the inverting terminal is 0 V. This circuit is an inverting transimpedance form, satisfying u0 = -Ix Rf. When S is connected to a, Rf = R1, and it is known that Ix = 5 mA and u0 = -5 V, therefore R1 = 5 V / 5 mA = 1 kΩ. When S is connected to b, Rf = R1 + R2, and it is known that Ix = 1 mA and u0 = -5 V, therefore R1 + R2 = 5 V / 1 mA = 5 kΩ. Thus R2 = 5 kΩ - 1 kΩ = 4 kΩ.

For S connected to a, identify Rf = R1 and use the text data u0 = -5 V when Ix = 5 mA to get R1 = 5 V / 5 mA = 1 kΩ. For S connected to b, identify Rf = R1 + R2 and use u0 = -5 V when Ix = 1 mA to get R1 + R2 = 5 V / 1 mA = 5 kΩ. Subtract to obtain R2 = 4 kΩ.

method.method_draft: Start by setting the inverting input voltage to 0 V because the + input is grounded and the ideal op amp is in feedback. In both switch positions, KCL at the inverting node gives the R1 current equal to Ix, so the voltage drop across R1 is Ix R1 from node a toward the virtual ground. When S is at a, node a is the output node, so u0 = -Ix R1; substituting Ix = 5 mA and u0 = -5 V gives R1 = 1 kΩ. When S is at b, the output is at node b; the same current Ix flows through R1 and R2 in series because op-amp input current is zero and the a branch is open, so u0 = -Ix(R1 + R2). Substituting Ix = 1 mA and u0 = -5 V gives R1 + R2 = 5 kΩ, hence R2 = 4 kΩ.
